On vessel segmentation, the learned erosions recover structuring elements that fit the vessels, as theoretically expected, whereas most of those trained with exact subgradients remain close to their initialisation.

items.title: RoboCode: Learning Reusable Action Primitives for Robot Manipulation
items.description: arXiv:2610.32225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent robot manipulation policies commonly predict continuous action chunks directly from observations, without explicitly modeling reusable structure in the action space. However, manipulation demonstrations often contain recurring short-horizon motion patterns that are shared across tasks. We introduce \textsc{RoboCode}, which learns these patterns through a shared soft-gated primitive action interface. Rather than assigning each action chunk to a single discrete code, \textsc{RoboCode} represents it as a soft composition of multiple learned primitives, providing a flexible intermediate representation of short-horizon actions. The primitive interface is learned from action chunks pooled across multiple tasks and then frozen while task-specific state encoders are trained to map current state inputs into the shared latent space. Experiments on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks address three questions. First, the learned primitive interface reconstructs action chunks with an average reconstruction MSE of 0.0187. Second, analysis of code activations reveals structured code reuse across tasks. Third, \textsc{RoboCode} achieves the highest or tied closed-loop success rate on all evaluated tasks, with an average success rate of 75.6%, compared with 68.8% for ACT and 41.6% for the larger Diffusion Policy baseline. These results suggest that soft-gated primitive codebooks provide an effective and interpretable intermediate action representation for robot manipulation.

items.title: TileShare: Training-Free Acceleration of Overlapping Tiled ViT Decoding
items.description: arXiv:2610.32233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fixed-window Vision Transformer (ViT) decoders run at deployment resolution as overlapping tiles: every token in an overlap band is processed by several full decoder instances. In the 2.4B-parameter MiniMax-H3 video decoder, about half of all per-token computation is duplicated. Removing the tiles fails because attention, global tokens and coordinates are bound to them. TileShare keeps each released tile's attention and computes every other operation once per token. The released computation changes at one kind of step only: an overlap token's per-tile results are blended into one shared state with the released weights. Interventions show that this blend costs quality where attention reads the shared states, mainly in the first few layers, which TileShare therefore keeps per tile. Without training, keeping six layers per tile decodes 1.38-1.51x faster than batched and compiled tiling on two GPU types (up to 1.96x with FP8) and is equivalent to the released decoder in PSNR, LPIPS and DISTS on DAVIS videos. On unseen UVG videos with the setting frozen beforehand, it matches PSNR and DISTS and improves LPIPS. TileShare carries over to two further decoders and is again confirmed on unseen data. It is equivalent in PSNR and DISTS on MAGI-1. On the ViTok-v2 image autoencoder at 2K-4K, it matches overlapping tiling in PSNR, improves LPIPS and DISTS and decodes 1.5-1.8x faster. How many layers stay per tile is measured once per model (for decoders, without labels); we report it for 14 decoders and encoders. Optionally, two GPU-hours of self-distillation let MiniMax-H3 share every layer without a loss in PSNR, and a coordinate field trained while the network stays frozen brings fully shared CLIP-based open-vocabulary segmentation to parity with sliding windows on seven benchmarks.

items.title: Empirical concentration for chains with infinite memory
items.description: arXiv:2610.32265v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Concentration inequalities for time series usually involve unknown quantities measuring dependence. This prevents their direct use as confidence bounds, or as criteria for learning algorithms. Recent works proved empirical concentration inequalities for stationary Markov chains, where the unknown quantities are estimated. We extend this approach beyond the Markov case, by considering stationary chains with infinite memory. We first establish a bounded-differences inequality on bounded Polish metric spaces under a summable Wasserstein contraction condition. We then estimate its dependence coefficients from a single trajectory, using either transition counts when the state space is finite, or derivatives of kernel conditional-density estimates for a continuous state space. We give general error bounds and illustrate their dependence on the memory tail. Finally, a fixed multiplicative safety factor turns these estimators into empirical concentration bounds. While some regularity assumptions are required to make the bounds empirical, our procedure remains fully adaptive in the sense that it does not require the knowledge of the constants involved in these assumptions. The empirical confidence bounds derived from our results are asymptotically as tight as the theoretical ones.

items.title: RootDown: Deploying and Benchmarking Models for Beet-Root Detection on Edge Devices
items.description: arXiv:2610.32275v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quality inspection of sugar beets after harvest and storage is critical to preserve sugar content and ensure optimal processing efficiency. The transfer of harvested beets to field clamps or trucks provides an opportunity to visually inspect individual beets automatically on loader conveyors. However, this is a challenging task as the large number of beets causes partial overlap and occlusion, complicating both annotation and detection. In this work, we propose an end-to-end image-based pipeline for detecting partially occluded sugar beets in loading scenarios as a first step toward automated quality inspection. We introduce a dedicated benchmark and present an automatic annotation strategy that leverages the SAM 3 foundation model to generate bounding boxes. We compare models trained on manually annotated and automatically generated labels. Additionally, we investigate deployment considerations by benchmarking multiple inference configurations, including execution on an edge device, under realistic operational constraints regarding precision, inference time and power consumption. Our results show that, despite substantial occlusion and inherent annotation ambiguity, foundation-model-based labels can substitute for a substantial share of manual annotation, trading labeling effort for data volume at a modest accuracy cost. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a Raspberry Pi 5 equipped with a Hailo accelerator enables high-performance, low-power inference, making it a practical solution for mobile outdoor deployment.

items.title: ReLEAP: Upcycling Vision Datasets through Cross-Task Unification and Semi-Supervised Annotation
items.description: arXiv:2610.32289v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Developing robust vision models requires large amounts of annotated data, especially for tasks involving fine-grained class distinctions under variable environmental conditions. Even in domains with numerous existing datasets, differences in annotation formats, label definitions and targeted learning tasks hinder data reuse and integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ReLEAP, a scalable Python framework for unifying heterogeneous image datasets through data-source abstraction, systematic reuse of annotations across learning tasks, and mapping of labels to a shared hierarchical taxonomy. We demonstrate its applicability in precision agriculture by integrating fifteen diverse datasets covering a broad range of plant species and annotation types. Beyond unification, ReLEAP enables systematic recycling of existing data and provides a robust foundation for learning-based annotation upcycling. Leveraging this foundation, we conduct extensive cross-dataset and fine-tuning experiments to investigate how domain-specific models trained on unified data and foundation models can be used to automatically generate higher-level annotations under unsupervised, weakly supervised and semi-supervised settings, and how dataset characteristics influence their effectiveness. Our results show that unified data access and annotation upcycling substantially expand the pool of reusable training data and annotations while improving data transparency, enabling more sustainable and resource-efficient use of existing datasets. We release the framework and trained models for academic use to support accessible and collaborative research, particularly in data-scarce and heterogeneous domains.

items.title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes
items.description: arXiv:2610.32299v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations remain a standard tool for aerodynamic analysis, yet each solve on an unstructured mesh is computationally expensive, making many-query tasks such as design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation costly. Neural operators provide mesh-flexible surrogates for mapping geometry and operating conditions to flow fields; however, in many existing architectures, global parameters such as the freestream state and design variables are concatenated with pointwise inputs, leaving their influence on intermediate features implicit. This paper proposes CoPiT, a \textbf{Co}nditional \textbf{P}osition-induced \textbf{T}ransformer that builds on the Position-induced Transformer (PiT) as its geometric backbone and injects a global condition vector through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), thereby making parametric modulation explicit while preserving geometry-based attention weights. The model is evaluated on two-dimensional AirfRANS airfoil fields, including scarce-data and extrapolation regimes, and on three-dimensional BlendedNet++ blended-wing-body surfaces. On the AirfRANS full-data test set, CoPiT reduces surface and volume losses by approximately 54\% and 24\% relative to Transolver, respectively, and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among the compared baselines on BlendedNet++. Matched ablations show that FiLM conditioning generally improves upon input concatenation, while the preferred placement is task-dependent. CoPiT thus provides a practical operator-learning surrogate for parametric aerodynamics on unstructured meshes.

items.title: Supervised Source Separation of Electric Vehicle Interior Noise Using a Hybrid Transformer Architecture
items.description: arXiv:2610.32310v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The interior sound of an electric vehicle is a superposition of several distinct noise contributions - wind noise, tire noise, powertrain (electric drive unit and inverter) noise, and auxiliary-drive noise - whose relative balance governs both the overall loudness and the perceived sound quality in the vehicle interior. Decomposing a recorded vehicle interior signal into these source contributions is a prerequisite for targeted acoustic engineering, but requires effortful measurement campaigns as well as expertise in the field of transfer path analysis. This work formulates the decomposition as a supervised, binaural source-separation problem with four target source contributions and adapts a hybrid time-spectrogram transformer architecture, originally developed for music demixing, to the domain of sound source separation for technical systems. To disambiguate source contributions, conditioning is introduced in the form of operating-state information, including electric drive speed, electric drive load, vehicle speed, and auxiliary-drive speed. Since isolated real-world reference stems are costly to obtain, the model is trained on a physics-based parametric data generator that synthesizes labeled component sounds from randomized virtual-vehicle hardware configurations and driving scenarios, so that the ground-truth contribution of each source is known by construction. Validation on both synthetic and measured vehicle interior sounds probes the achieved separation performance and underscores the feasibility of applying the proposed method for acoustic contribution analysis in technical systems.

items.title: GeoLEON-CLIP: Graph-Anchored Multimodal Contrastive Learning for Geographic Region Representation
items.description: arXiv:2610.32311v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Geographic regions are multimodal: satellite imagery captures visual morphology, text conveys human-interpretable semantics, and map structures describe urban context. Existing geospatial contrastive methods typically align image-text or image-location pairs, underusing structured map data. We introduce GeoLEON-CLIP, a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns three views of each H3-indexed region: an OpenStreetMap-derived graph embedding, a satellite image crop, and a textual description. Frozen pretrained LEON graph embeddings provide a semantic anchor between vision and language. Frozen graph, image, and text encoders are connected by trainable residual projection heads and trained with a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective. Experiments show strong graph-image and graph-text alignment; graph-image retrieval achieves the best cross-modal performance in a mixed-resolution pool. To evaluate the anchoring hypothesis, we propose chained cross-modal recall $\mathrm{R}@A@B$, which routes retrieval through the graph modality and compares it with direct retrieval under a matched candidate budget. At $\mathrm{R}@1@1$, image$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$text and text$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$image outperform direct image-text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points, respectively, despite using a single intermediate cell. Downstream probes show task-dependent gains, with the largest improvements on Airbnb and Beijing housing. These results indicate that OpenStreetMap graph structure can anchor multimodal representations combining maps, imagery, and language.

items.title: KnitTrans: Coordinated Trajectory Transfer for Effective and Efficient LLM Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.32389v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Trajectory transfer from rollout to training affects both learning quality and system efficiency in large language model reinforcement learning (RL). Enforcing batch-wide training requirements can delay the admission of completed trajectories, resulting in higher architectural staleness: the additional parameter-version gap from disaggregated pipelining relative to colocated execution. Beyond admission, misalignment between data access and training consumption causes redundant movement and unnecessary waiting when transferring large trajectory payloads. We present KnitTrans, a system that coordinates the rollout-to-training path through three designs. First, constraint-preserving mini-batch admission allows flexibility in early mini-batch composition, while checking that enough capacity remains to satisfy the remaining quotas. Second, on-demand trajectory data access matches storage units to consumer assignments and overlaps micro-batch data preparation with computation. Third, multimodal encoding deduplication supports reuse across a mini-batch while preserving gradient contributions from all backbone micro-batches. Experiments show up to 93% lower architectural staleness than with train-batch admission, narrowing the learning-quality gap between disaggregated execution and colocated execution. On multimodal workloads, KnitTrans reduces transfer latency by two orders of magnitude and achieves a speedup of up to 5.8 times in transfer plus training over the baseline.

items.title: On the Limits of Stochastic Push-Pull over Time-Varying Digraphs
items.description: arXiv:2610.32422v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stochastic Push-Pull achieves linear speedup with respect to the network size $n$ on static strongly connected digraphs, but whether this speedup persists on time-varying networks remains unclear. In this work, we construct a quadratic decentralized problem on period-two networks showing that stochastic Push-Pull may fail to attain linear speedup over time-varying digraphs. For $p$-periodic networks, we identify an effective node count $n_{\mathrm{eff}}\le n$ that governs the leading stochastic term. Specifically, for smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish convergence upper bounds and matching lower bounds for stochastic Push-Pull with constant stepsizes, both exhibiting the leading-order dependence $\Theta(1/\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{eff}} T})$. When $p=1$, the identity $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=n$ recovers the usual linear speedup for static digraphs. However, periodic networks can have $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=o(n)$, demonstrating the loss of linear speedup under temporal variation. Numerical experiments illustrate effective-count scaling and the separation between static and periodic networks, consistent with our theoretical findings.

items.title: PROVE: Probabilistic Visual Grounding via Patch-Level Evidence for Vision-Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.32440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual grounding with vision-language models such as CLIP typically produces a single deterministic relevance map for an image-query pair, without indicating whether the localisation is reliable or whether the referent is present at all. We introduce \textbf{PROVE} (\textbf{Pro}babilistic \textbf{V}isual Grounding via Patch-Level \textbf{E}vidence), a post-hoc evidential adapter that maps frozen CLIP patch features to per-patch Beta distributions without modifying the backbone. PROVE casts grounding as per-patch membership: each patch accumulates positive and negative evidence for whether it belongs to the referent, so a query may match zero, one, or many patches. We train PROVE with an evidential objective on soft patch-coverage targets, and define a prior-pull objective that keeps absent-referent examples near an uninformative prior, so that vacuity serves as an absence signal without a dedicated presence classifier. During inference, a single forward pass yields, in closed form, a posterior-mean grounding map, a spatial vacuity map, and an image-level absence score. We evaluate PROVE on referring-expression benchmarks: it is competitive in localisation with state-of-the-art CLIP grounding methods, its uncertainty tracks localisation error and supports selective prediction under abstention, and its image-level score detects when the referent is absent altogether. Our evidential patch-membership modelling offers a simple, drop-in mechanism for probabilistic verification in frozen vision-language grounding systems.

items.title: PathJev: Decision-Native Vision-Language Modelling for Histopathology
items.description: arXiv:2610.32478v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models used for decisions in histopathology rarely return calibrated probabilities over the candidates a user cares about. Decision-native models write a question and a candidate set chosen at run time into the input and return a normalised distribution from a small decision head in one forward pass. We build PathJev-P, a decision-native model for histopathology: MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head, trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections whose expert labels are turned into typed questions with organ-specific candidate sets and a "none of these" option. In a comparison over 3 seeds with an analysis plan fixed before testing, on test sets without documented overlap with the training data of the backbone, PathJev-P is more accurate than a generative model trained with the same backbone, data and selection rule, the zero-shot pathology model CONCH and a general medical decision model (balanced accuracy 0.541 against 0.492, 0.345 and 0.213); its advantage over the generative model comes from two organs absent from training. The calibration advantage depends on how the generative model's probabilities are read out. With the summed candidate log-likelihood used in previous work, PathJev-P has the lower calibration error (ECE 0.204 against 0.279); with a length-normalised read-out of the same generative model, examined post hoc, the two have similar mean calibration error (0.201) and the generative model is better calibrated on the unseen organs, where PathJev-P remains over-confident. A supervised linear probe on a pathology foundation model is better calibrated in every setting. In a qualitative whole-slide demonstration, PathJev-P labels unsupervised tissue clusters with abstention and separates carcinoma from other tissue while running the model on a fraction of the tiles.

items.title: State Estimation as In-context Tabular Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2610.32487v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This letter poses state estimation (SE) as an in-context tabular prediction (ICTP) problem. The key idea is a tabular arrangement in which historical measurement vectors and corresponding state estimates serve as the context, and a new measurement vector forms the query for which we predict a state vector. We propose to use tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained on synthetic data, whose weights are never updated, so power system data is needed only as context. With frozen TFM weights we estimate the state of 14-, 30-, 33-, 70-, and 118-bus transmission and distribution networks, and do so where weighted least squares (WLS) fails or degrades, under low observability and with bad data. ICTP errors are 11 to 57$\times$ below the per-bus average of the context at full metering, and 1.3 to 4.0$\times$ below it with only 5% of measurements available. With measurements at six buses biased by 8$\sigma$, the ICTP angle error rises 1.8 to 5.0$\times$ over its bias-free value against 2.5 to 12.7$\times$ for WLS with bad-data detection. Without retraining, ICTP has lower voltage error than DSS$^2$ on both of its feeders, and lower than a retrained TAPINE on two of three reconfiguration sets.

items.title: Random Jump Forests
items.description: arXiv:2610.32498v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Random jump forests are introduced as a nonparametric tool for estimating conditional cumulative transition rates and occupation probabilities in multi-state models. The main idea is that a single tree partitions the covariate space for all transitions simultaneously, using partially observed trajectories, and with Nelson--Aalen estimators at the terminal nodes. Occupation probabilities are recovered through the product integral without requiring the Markov assumption. Uniform consistency and a functional central limit theorem for the estimators of cumulative rates can be established under the assumption that the covariate vector takes finitely many values, and under suitable splitting conditions. In particular, pointwise confidence intervals and simultaneous bands are available in the Markov case. Simulation studies show a predictive accuracy close to the correctly specified benchmark models and marked improvements when benchmarks are misspecified, with further illustration on four biomedical data sets. In the coverage study, confidence bands attain near-nominal coverage in several settings, with pooling of heterogeneous rates being the main source of possible undercoverage. The method, including prediction assessment and variable importance, is implemented in the R package JumpForests.

items.title: Quantum-Classical Link Prediction on Dark Web Hyperlink Graphs
items.description: arXiv:2610.32510v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We analyze HTML content and hyperlinks from an offline Tor crawl containing 383 onion hosts and 2,067 directed cross-host links. The study combines semantic analysis with degree-controlled quantum--classical link prediction. Two directory groups emit 94.8\% of the observed host links. Directed preferential attachment reaches ROC-AUC 0.976 with random non-edges, but falls to $0.550\pm0.014$ under source-conditioned target-degree matching. With disjoint training and test pairs, multimodal logistic regression reaches $0.672\pm0.021$, GAE $0.899\pm0.016$, and VGAE $0.906\pm0.016$. A four-qubit variational quantum classifier (VQC) comparison tests two encodings across 20 disjoint-pair graph splits under exact and 1,024-shot simulation, with classical controls using the same inputs and training examples. Its best exact mean ROC-AUC is $0.549\pm0.023$, compared with $0.551\pm0.016$ for RBF SVC and $0.573\pm0.029$ for a 16-parameter MLP on the same inputs and training examples. These results support predictive signal in combined graph/content features and show why degree control, feature compression, and optimization conditions matter in quantum--classical comparisons.

items.title: Exact Global Minimax Risk near Nonidentification
items.description: arXiv:2610.32546v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study squared-error estimation when a nuisance parameter is unidentified on a submodel but affects a target that vanishes there. For models with higher-order profile expansions, we give sufficient conditions under which the largest critical-path minimax risk is the exact asymptotic minimax risk over the full parameter space. An efficient observable feature, negligible calibration error and stable recovery yield one estimator attaining the leading constant uniformly, with the profile coordinates unknown. The estimator uses calibration estimates, a local feature mean and an empirical recovery feature. The constant is expressed through a bounded-normal decision problem. We verify the conditions in two models. In centered Gaussian logistic errors-in-variables regression with one surrogate and two unknown variances, we determine the fifth-order global coefficient risk and its exact constant. A sparse extension separates variance-decomposition uncertainty from direction estimation and specifies when the scalar constant is preserved. In a degree-balanced replicated-network model, we determine the sixth-order global edge-contrast risk when block proportions are unknown. Triangles identify a parameter combination; a bowtie supplies the additional information needed for the contrast.

items.title: Batched NN 4D-Var: a performant hybrid model framework for the Integrated Forecasting System
items.description: arXiv:2610.32582v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hybrid forecasting systems combining machine learning and numerical weather prediction offer a promising route toward improved forecast skill while preserving physical consistency. In this study, we investigate online learning of state-dependent model-error corrections within the Integrated Forecasting System using 4D-Var. Building on previous work, we represent model error using a neural network embedded within the forecast model and trained from observations through the data assimilation cycle. First, we introduce a targeted variant of neural-network 4D-Var in which only the neural-network parameters are estimated, while the atmospheric state is provided by a precomputed analysis. We then propose a batched extension that processes assimilation windows in random order and averages parameter increments over multiple windows, drawing inspiration from mini-batch stochastic optimization. Experiments are conducted with the Integrated Forecasting System of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts at an intermediate resolution. Sequential online learning substantially improves forecasts within the training period, with error reductions exceeding 10%in some cases. However, these improvements fail to generalize to unseen data. In contrast, the proposed batched formulation produces hybrid models that consistently improve forecast skill in out-of-sample experiments. Larger batch sizes accelerate convergence and improve robustness by reducing the noise of parameter updates. Diagnostics further show that the online-trained corrections preserve realistic forecast variability and do not improve skill through artificial smoothing. These results demonstrate that the formulation of the online learning problem is critical for generalisation and establish batched online training as a promising framework for hybrid machine-learning/data-assimilation systems.

items.title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes
items.description: arXiv:2610.32598v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symmetric polyconvexity provides a sufficient condition for weak lower semicontinuity in small-strain elasticity and a tractable lower bound for the relaxation of non-(quasi)convex energies. Since classical algorithms for computing such functions can be computationally expensive, neural network approximations have recently emerged as an alternative. A central difficulty with establishing such neural network based approaches for symmetric polyconvexity is the additional monotonicity property. As we show, the corresponding weight restrictions on ReLU-based input-convex networks do not yield universal approximation of the lifted representers. Here, we introduce symmetric polyconvex neural networks (SPCNNs) for constitutive modeling and approximation of symmetric polyconvex envelopes. The deep architecture combines convexity with the monotonicity required of a representer in the space of minors. We prove a universal approximation theorem for symmetric polyconvex energies, without requiring isotropy, and quantify the number of affine pieces attainable by the lifted network and derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies. Numerical examples illustrate stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential. Symmetric polyconvexity is guaranteed by construction, while the accuracy of the fitted energies and envelopes is assessed numerically.

items.title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!
items.description: arXiv:2610.32601v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid turbulence, a chaotic and non-linear physical phenomenon characterized by complex eddies interacting across vast spatial and temporal scales. A numerically accurate modeling of this multi-scale energy cascade requires fully resolving both the fine spatial structures and the continuous temporal evolution of the flow field. In this paper, we leverage massive, time-resolved direct numerical simulations, which exceed 28 TB per run, to assess how numerical choices govern the resolved (3+1)-dimensional physics of turbulent flows. Building on this analysis, we study how neural networks represent the recorded turbulent motion. Our results highlight that spatial and temporal assessments can disagree for both numerical records and learned representations. We therefore call on the machine learning community to treat (3+1)-dimensional turbulence as a four-dimensional phenomenon.

items.title: Acquisition for Spherical-Linear Bayesian Optimization on the Cube
items.description: arXiv:2610.32628v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work demonstrated that executing Bayesian Optimization (BO) using simply a linear surrogate with a clever transformation is enough to approximate the performance of the standard Gaussian-Process (GP) based version on high-dimensional test functions. When the decision region is a sphere, this strategy admits rapid exact acquisition. However, it is the unit cube we encounter most often in the BO literature, and in this setting a standard approach, namely a multi-start quasi-Newton method, is employed for solving the acquisition subproblem. In this article, we will discuss a series of results, both positive and negative, regarding the complexity of global resolution of various acquisition subproblems over the unit cube. On the basis of this discussion, we will propose a new acquisition function which is globally optimizable using significantly less execution time than the incumbent approach while maintaining or improving performance. The resulting method is competitive with GP-based BO in terms of accuracy per evaluation, and is superior in terms of accuracy per walltime on black-boxes of low to moderate computational intensity.

items.title: EMG Tokenization Preserves Movement Information at a Fraction of the Bitrate
items.description: arXiv:2610.32674v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wireless electromyography (EMG) interfaces must balance electrode coverage against transmission bandwidth. Here, we show that compact EMG tokens substantially reduce payload while retaining information for three-dimensional hand-pose decoding. We evaluate two causal tokenizers fitted without pose labels: an encoder pretrained to reconstruct EMG spectra and one based on SPAR, an engineered spectral-spatial representation of neighbouring electrodes. In personalized, within-session experiments with 320-channel EMG from nine participants, we compare tokenized and continuous features using matched decoder architectures and training procedures. Averaged across decoders, tokenization changed mean error by +0.01 mm for SPAR (95% confidence interval: -0.12 to 0.14) and +0.45 mm for the learned representation (0.10 to 0.82). Both increases met a 1 mm non-inferiority criterion. Stored token arrays reduced payloads 41-fold relative to raw EMG and 36-fold relative to continuous SPAR features. On sampled windows of the public emg2pose benchmark's test partition, absolute differences in mean error between learned tokens and continuous features were below 0.05 mm across 176 participants and in the subset of 20 participants unseen during training. Electrode coverage, calibration, and unseen recordings affected SPAR decoding more than quantization did. In a computational benchmark, optimized SPAR generated tokens for 63 channels within 20 ms on a Cortex-M55 microcontroller. These findings support tokenization as a compact interface between wearable sensing and movement decoding, allowing decoders to be updated while the wearable encoder and transmitted representation remain fixed.

items.title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials
items.description: arXiv:2610.32678v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Crystal materials are designed either by screening known crystals for a target property or by generating new crystals with that property. Both routes are judged against public databases of known crystals, but these databases name the same crystal differently. Several materials announced as new by recent generative and autonomous discovery campaigns have since proved to be known phases or close variants of them. The limits of both routes remain unmeasured. Here we probe them by matching the crystals of 55 databases by structure into one self-extending database of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values, each traced to its source. Only 4.5% of its crystal-property pairs carry a value. To fill the empty pairs, we developed CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer with state-of-the-art accuracy on several tasks of two public benchmarks. Trained on each task, it forms a library of property models whose predictions we release. The reach of forward screening has been underestimated. Known crystals hold tens of thousands of ultra-incompressible candidates without a recorded bulk modulus, and a post hoc audit of synthesis evidence finds among them ReN2, whose bulk modulus was measured at 428 GPa. The novelty claimed for inverse design has been overestimated. At an equal verification budget, a stiffness-conditioned generator returned more stiff hits than screening (100 versus 55), but all contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions. Integrating and completing the databases of known crystals therefore moves the limits of both routes: it widens what screening can reach and sets the reference against which generated crystals are judged new.

items.title: Score-Preserving Continual Lasso under Task Shift
items.description: arXiv:2610.32708v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to learn from sequential tasks while mitigating catastrophic forgetting when historical data are no longer accessible. We study continual learning for high-dimensional sparse linear regression, where $\ell_1$ regularization creates a difficulty absent from continual ridge regression: that recursively reusing an $\ell_1$-penalized estimator can propagate earlier shrinkage and accumulate regularization bias across tasks. We propose score-preserving continual Lasso (SP-CL), which separates sparse estimation from state transmission by preserving the historical squared-loss score. Under squared loss, its cumulative estimator exactly recovers a full-history Lasso minimizer. When task coefficients coincide, it inherits the full-history sparse rate. For related task-specific coefficients, SP-CL uses a regularized current-task correction that leaves the transmitted state unchanged and attains the offline source-assisted rate under an oracle related-task condition. We also derive Overall/BWT/FWT decompositions that distinguish historical information loss, task conflict, and current-task specialization, and validate the resulting regimes in simulation.

items.title: Cross-Scenario Controller Parameter Transformation from Real-World Driving Data through Flow Matching
items.description: arXiv:2610.32719v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems have become increasingly widespread, aiming to support drivers, reduce workload, and improve traffic safety. However, many systems are rarely used because their behavior feels unnatural and does not match individual driving behavior. The growing availability of large-scale, real-world human driving data enables more human-like and driver-individual assistance functions. This paper formulates the adaptation of Adaptive Cruise Control parameters as a driver-individual scenario-to-scenario transport problem, transforming controller parameters from one driving context to another. Using flow matching, we train a generative model to predict the target-scenario behavior of previously unseen drivers from only a few demonstrations in a source scenario. We compare the approach with a linear parameter-shift baseline and evaluate flow-matching variants incorporating driver-consistent coupling, driver embeddings, and classifier-free guidance based on driving profiles extracted from trajectory data using a variational autoencoder.

items.title: Sparse Bayesian Neural Networks via Sticky Piecewise Deterministic Markov Processes
items.description: arXiv:2610.32753v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: There is growing evidence that the performance of a neural network depends largely on a small subset of its weights, which are typically identified by training a dense network and pruning it afterwards. Within a Bayesian framework, pruning can be directly incorporated through a spike-and-slab prior, providing a proper treatment of the uncertainties involved, both with respect to pruning and to parameter uncertainty. In Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), sampling by MCMC is notoriously hard. We demonstrate that modern Monte Carlo methods based on piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) can be used to sample posteriors of BNNs asymptotically exact whenever numerically constructed rate bounds hold. Spike-and-slab priors can be incorporated through sticky versions of the PDMPs, setting weights exactly to zero during sampling. We examine the predictive performance and convergence of the samplers, and show that sparse BNNs sampled this way can be more robust to input noise than dense ones.

items.title: ARENA: Active Region attENtion Aggregation for interpretable solar flare prediction
items.description: arXiv:2610.32758v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting solar flares is a challenging space-weather forecasting problem with potentially significant impacts on Earth's upper atmosphere, including disruptions to radio communications. We propose Active Region attENtion Aggregation (ARENA), a neural network architecture that predicts solar flares from a variable number of active-region cutouts while learning to identify the region most relevant to the prediction. ARENA is trained using multiple-instance learning under weak supervision, requiring only a flare/no-flare label for the observation and no labels specifying the flare origin. The learned attention mechanism therefore provides a means of localizing the active region driving the prediction without explicit origin annotations. ARENA achieves a heidke skill score of 0.45 which is comparable to other flare prediction approaches. These results demonstrate that active-region-based aggregation can provide an efficient and interpretable approach to solar flare prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LuisBauer22/ARENA.

items.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
items.description: arXiv:2610.32788v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $\alpha=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $\alpha/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $\alpha_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.

items.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
items.description: arXiv:2610.32854v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. Under a local linearization, LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback--Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance, constructed from activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression; when its kernel meets these directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters change the singular geometry. We characterize this geometry locally through observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally through affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. The global learning complexity need not be determined at a ground-truth parameter, as singularities on another rank stratum can dominate. We also introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT. Experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.

items.title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
items.description: arXiv:2610.32876v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way.

items.title: When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation
items.description: arXiv:2610.32888v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.

items.title: LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders
items.description: arXiv:2610.32894v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons.

items.title: Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time
items.description: arXiv:2610.32940v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the fundamental problem of PAC learning positive linear combinations of $k$ arbitrary ReLU activations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to the Gaussian distribution, in $L_2$ loss. We give the first fully-polynomial time algorithm for this learning task. Specifically, our algorithm draws $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/\epsilon)$ samples, runs in $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/\epsilon)$ time, and outputs a hypothesis that is $\epsilon$-close to the target concept with high probability. All prior algorithms for this problem require super-polynomial time in $k$ or $1/\epsilon$, or leverage strong well-conditioned assumptions on the weight matrix. On a technical level, our approach develops a novel boosting procedure of a ``weak'' learner that recovers the hidden weight vectors to constant error, in a list-decodable manner. To develop this ``weak'' learning procedure, we leverage implicit tensor computation techniques to construct a low-degree filtering procedure based on Hermite tensors of the target function. This procedure amplifies separation among (clusters of) weight vectors to learn each of them to constant error. We then argue that the same procedure can be used for improving the estimation of hidden weight vectors, using gradient descent-like updates on the Euclidean sphere. A crucial ingredient of our algorithm is a pruning approach that ensures only relevant vectors that approximate the hidden weight vectors at target accuracy are maintained by the algorithm.

items.title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
items.description: arXiv:2610.32941v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $\pi$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $\pi$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.

items.title: Knowledge Distillation across Item and Code Spaces for Parallel Generative Recommendation
items.description: arXiv:2610.32943v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative recommendation with semantic IDs represents each item as a sequence of discrete codes derived from its semantic representation and predicts these codes to generate recommendations. Existing semantic-ID recommenders are typically trained with hard labels for the observed next item. Although such supervision identifies the target, it provides no explicit distributional information about alternative items conditioned on the same user history. Sequential recommenders can supply this item-level predictive knowledge, but transferring it to semantic-ID generation is challenging because the teacher and student operate in item and code spaces, respectively. We propose two complementary knowledge-distillation objectives for parallel semantic-ID recommenders, which predict all code positions simultaneously without autoregressive prefix conditioning. Item Distribution Matching (IDM) reconstructs a catalogue-level item distribution from the student's parallel code predictions and aligns it with the teacher's item distribution. Code Marginal Matching (CMM) projects the teacher's item probabilities onto each code position using fixed item-to-code assignments, then matches the resulting code marginals to the corresponding student heads. Both objectives transfer the teacher's soft distributional knowledge while preserving the student's parallel prediction structure. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that both methods consistently outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches. On average, IDM improves Recall@10 by 15.39%, while CMM improves NDCG@10 by 8.28%. These results demonstrate that distillation in either reconstructed item space or code-marginal space can substantially strengthen hard-label supervision for parallel generative recommendation.

items.title: Flownomaly: Single-Step Conditional-Mean Recovery for Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
items.description: arXiv:2610.32964v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Few-shot industrial anomaly detection requires modeling category-specific normality from only a handful of defect-free images. Common approaches tie inference to stored exemplars, impose rigid linear structure, or risk reproducing anomalous content. Flownomaly instead casts the problem as normal-counterpart recovery in frozen DINOv2 feature space. Given normal supports, a velocity field is learned through conditional flow matching over frozen patch tokens to transport Gaussian noise toward normal features. Along straight paths, a single recovery step using one evaluation of the optimal field yields the posterior mean of the clean normal token without trajectory integration. The operating time governs how strongly recovery modifies a query token. With no anomalous validation samples available for tuning, a normal-only Jacobian gain-to-noise criterion selects this time from the supports alone. Squared residuals between query tokens and their recovered counterparts yield anomaly signals for both dense localization and image-level detection. Across 1-, 2-, and 4-shot benchmarks on MVTec-AD and VisA, together with sample-shot evaluations on Real-IAD, Flownomaly achieves state-of-the-art performance against recent category-specific methods. In the 1-shot setting, image- and pixel-level AUROC reach 97.8% and 98.0% on MVTec-AD and 95.3% and 98.7% on VisA, with a 2.1-point image-level AUROC improvement over the strongest baseline on VisA. Code is available at https://github.com/b-rbmp/Flownomaly.

items.title: Maximum Likelihood on the Joint (Data, Condition) Distribution for Solving Ill-Posed Problems with Conditional Flow Models
items.description: arXiv:2208.11782v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the absence of conditioning information, normalizing flow models are trained using maximum likelihood. Previous extensions to conditional settings have abandoned the simple maximum-likelihood approach, as obtaining the full joint distribution of data and conditions for training purposes (or equivalently, the true conditional distribution for each point in the training dataset) is impossible. However, under special conditions that nevertheless apply to a wide class of useful problems, it is possible to obtain a simple, computationally cheap proxy with the same global minimum as the conditional likelihood. Conditional flow models trained using this proxy do not require explicit knowledge of the conditional distribution, auxiliary networks or other specific architecture, or additional loss terms beyond maximum likelihood. They provide a natural and powerful way to solve a class of ill-posed inverse problems. I demonstrate these properties on easily visualized toy problems, then use the method to successfully generate class-conditional images and to reconstruct semantically degraded images via super-resolution.

items.title: FC-PINO: High Precision Physics-Informed Neural Operators via Fourier Continuation
items.description: arXiv:2211.15960v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The physics-informed neural operator (PINO) is a machine learning paradigm that has demonstrated promising results for learning solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs). It leverages the Fourier Neural Operator to learn solution operators in function spaces and leverages physics losses during training to penalize deviations from known physics laws. Spectral differentiation provides an efficient way to compute derivatives for the physics losses, but it inherently assumes periodicity. When applied to non-periodic functions, this assumption can lead to significant errors, including Gibbs phenomena near domain boundaries which degrade the accuracy of both function representations and derivative computations. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the FC-PINO (Fourier-Continuation-based Physics-Informed Neural Operator) architecture which extends the accuracy and efficiency of PINO and spectral differentiation to non-periodic and non-smooth PDEs. In FC-PINO, we propose integrating Fourier continuation into the PINO framework, and test two different continuation approaches: FC-Legendre and FC-Gram. By transforming non-periodic signals into periodic functions on extended domains in a well-conditioned manner, Fourier continuation enables fast and accurate derivative computations. This approach avoids the discretization sensitivity of finite differences and the memory overhead of automatic differentiation. We demonstrate that standard PINO fails (without padding) or struggles (even with padding) to solve non-periodic and non-smooth PDEs with high precision, across challenging benchmarks. In contrast, the proposed FC-PINO provides accurate, robust, and scalable solutions, substantially outperforming PINO alternatives, and demonstrating that Fourier continuation is critical for extending PINO to a wider range of PDE problems when high-precision solutions are needed.

items.title: Learning from Hypervectors: A Survey on Hyperdimensional Encoding
items.description: arXiv:2308.00685v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is an emerging computing paradigm that imitates the brain's structure to offer a powerful and efficient processing and learning model. In HDC, the data are encoded with long vectors, called hypervectors, which typically range from 1,000 to 10,000 in length. The literature provides several encoding methods to generate orthogonal or correlated hypervectors, based on the application. Existing surveys focus on overall HDC system aspects like inputs, primary computations, and outputs. However, this study takes a more specific approach. It zeroes in on the HDC system input and the generation of hypervectors, directly influencing the hypervector encoding. This survey brings together various hypervector generation and encoding methods, exploring the limitations, challenges, and potential benefits they entail.

items.title: From Dueling Bandits to Episodic MDPs: Learning with Adversarial Preference Feedback
items.description: arXiv:2507.11706v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In dueling bandits, the learner compares two arms in each round and observes only which one is preferred. This paper asks what changes when the compared pair also affects the next state, as in a recommendation interface where the pair shown to a user affects the user's next context. We formulate this problem as a state-wise preference-based MDP, an episodic tabular MDP in which the learner selects a pair of arms at each visited state, observes only a noisy comparison between them, and moves to a next state that may depend on the pair. The preferences may change adversarially across episodes, and the loss of a pair is defined through Borda scores. We show that the minimax regret of this problem under known transitions is $\tilde{\Theta}(\min\{HT,(H^3SK)^{1/3}T^{2/3}\})$, where $H$, $S$, $K$, and $T$ are the numbers of steps per episode, states, arms, and episodes, and that this rate is achieved by an algorithm based on online linear optimization over the set of occupancy measures. If the pair did not affect the next state, each state would be a separate dueling bandit, and the $T^{2/3}$ term of the minimax regret would be smaller by a factor of $H^{1/3}$, demonstrating the cost of having action-dependent state transitions. We also give a policy optimization algorithm with closed-form updates, whose regret is $\tilde{O}((H^4SK^3)^{1/3}T^{2/3})$ up to lower-order terms, and we extend both algorithms to unknown transitions.

items.title: Clip-Low Increases Entropy and Clip-High Decreases Entropy in Reinforcement Learning of Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2509.26114v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently emerged as the leading approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, RLVR is prone to entropy collapse, where the LLM quickly converges to a near-deterministic form, hindering exploration and progress during prolonged RL training. In this work, we reveal that the clipping mechanism in PPO and GRPO induces biases on entropy. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, we show that clip-low increases entropy, while clip-high decreases it. Further, under standard clipping parameters, the effect of clip-high dominates, resulting in an overall entropy reduction even when purely random rewards are provided to the RL algorithm. Our findings highlight an overlooked confounding factor in RLVR: independent of the reward signal, the clipping mechanism influences entropy, which in turn affects the reasoning behavior. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that clipping can be deliberately used to control entropy. Specifically, with a more aggressive clip-low value, one can increase entropy, promote exploration, and ultimately prevent entropy collapse in RLVR training.

items.title: Iterative Policy Optimization: Batch-Online Multi-Turn RL via Single-Turn RL
items.description: arXiv:2511.21638v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Practical LLM agents often operate over multi-turn conversations where success is determined only after the full interaction ends. Most multi-turn RL methods train via on-policy rollouts, but unlike in single-turn RL, the policy cannot produce a trajectory alone, since an external environment must respond after each agent turn. For conversational agents, this environment is a user, but real users are generally unavailable inside the training loop and simulated users are difficult to build faithfully. Separately, real-world deployment is rarely fully online or fully offline. The common production pattern is called batch online, where the current policy is deployed to collect a batch of interaction data, then retrained on that batch and redeployed. We show that this batch-online setting creates an opportunity for applying the classical approximate policy iteration algorithm. Our central observation is that running standard token-level, single-turn GRPO with a learned turn-level $Q$-function as the reward model is a policy improvement step for the multi-turn problem. Building on this, we present Iterative Policy Optimization (IterPO), which alternates between fitting $Q^\pi$ from logged Monte Carlo returns via standard reward modeling (policy evaluation) and running single-turn GRPO against $Q^\pi$ (policy improvement). During policy improvement, the learned $Q^\pi$ scores candidate responses by their expected downstream return, avoiding the need for simulator rollouts of the remaining conversation. Overall, this allows us to do principled multi-turn RL using only single-turn RL methods without an interactive environment or user simulator inside the training loop. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IterPO on six multi-turn negotiation environments.

items.title: Softly Symbolifying Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
items.description: arXiv:2512.07875v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (KANs) offer a promising path toward interpretable machine learning: their learnable activations can be studied individually while collectively fitting complex data accurately. In practice, however, trained activations often lack *symbolic fidelity*, learning pathological decompositions with no meaningful correspondence to interpretable forms. We propose Softly Symbolified Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (S2KAN), which integrate symbolic primitives directly into training. Each activation draws from a dictionary of symbolic and dense terms, with learnable gates that sparsify the representation. Crucially, this sparsification is differentiable, enabling end-to-end optimization, and uses an optimization objective inspired by minimum description length. S2KAN can discover interpretable activation functions while retaining dense splines for flexible approximation. We introduce a quantitative measure of symbolic fidelity, assessing how closely learned activations can be approximated by short expressions from a specified symbolic language. Across real-world prediction tasks, dynamical-system forecasting, and synthetic symbolic benchmarks, S2KAN generally achieves higher symbolic fidelity and often far smaller models, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy on real-world data and low prediction errors on most symbolic benchmark configurations. We also examine the models' learned responses on scientific data, including the contributions of their symbolic components. Together, these results show that incorporating symbolic structure during training can yield compact, accurate KAN models whose learned responses can be examined through their symbolic components.

items.title: Multi-Task Learning for Metal Alloy Property Prediction: An Empirical Study of Negative Transfer and Mitigation Strategies
items.description: arXiv:2512.22740v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) in materials science relies on the assumption that physically related properties share learnable representations. We challenge this assumption using a 54,028-sample metal alloy dataset exhibiting extreme task-level imbalance. Our results reveal a striking dichotomy: MTL significantly degrades regression performance for resistivity and hardness but improves classification recall for amorphous-forming ability. We trace this divergence to mismatched functional forms--such as resistivity's polynomial dependence versus hardness's complex interactions--which cause severe gradient misalignment during optimization. Evaluating Deep Imbalanced Regression techniques, we find that projecting conflicting gradients (PCGrad) recovers single-task performance, while combining label distribution smoothing with gradient normalization achieves the best overall balance. Consequently, we propose a strategic framework: utilize independent models for high-precision characterization, but employ MTL for high-throughput screening where recall is paramount. These findings support a "materials property clustering" hypothesis, suggesting that distinct physical mechanisms require specialized optimization strategies to overcome negative transfer.

items.title: On the Runway Cascade of Transformers for Language Modeling
items.description: arXiv:2601.14522v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In decoder-only (causal) transformers, the computation graph created by causal masking routes information through both direct-path attention and indirect paths formed by intermediate tokens. We denote these indirect paths between token pairs as their runways. We argue that certain failure modes of causal transformers as observed by a growing body of recent works are likely exacerbated by a misalignment between these two information propagation modes. We formalize runway cascade as a phenomenon whereby this misalignment results in redundancies and irrelevant information cascading to token representations despite adequately learned attention patterns. As a solution, we propose runway-aware rewiring as a more explicit way of incorporating runway context directly into each token's direct-path attention. This mechanism re-wires the attention pattern for each token based on a summary of its runway landscape, enabling awareness of accumulating representational influences and allowing for more balanced information propagation. Our proposed methodology introduces no additional parameters and can seamlessly be integrated into standard attention mechanism. Empirically, our rewired transformer results in steady improvements in general language modeling as well as noticeably stronger information retrieval and extrapolation abilities compared to standard transformers.

items.title: Feature-Space Smoothing: Certified Robustness of Deep Representations
items.description: arXiv:2601.16200v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern deep learning models exhibit strong capabilities across diverse applications, yet remain vulnerable to malicious inputs that induce erroneous predictions via feature-space distortion. To address that, we propose Feature-Space Smoothing (FS), a representation-level certification framework built upon Gaussian randomized smoothing. We show that FS converts a given feature encoder into a smoothed variant that is guaranteed to maintain a certified lower bound on the cosine similarity between clean and adversarial features under l_2-bounded perturbations. We then establish that this Feature Cosine Similarity Bound (FCSB) can be extended to the prediction-wise certification under the cosine similarity measure, and the value of FCSB is determined by the encoder intrinsic Gaussian robustness score. Building on those insights, we introduce the Gaussian Smoothness Booster (GSB), a plug-and-play module to improve the encoder Gaussian robustness score. Specifically, the GSB module is plugged to enhance the feature-space consistency and maintain the feature utility for downstream tasks under Gaussian perturbations. This design enables seamless integration of FS on the protected model, e.g., Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), without additional model retraining or alignment, improving its robustness while preserving the performance for downstream task-oriented decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating FS consistently provides non-trivial certified robustness and significantly improves task-oriented performance under strong white-box adversarial attacks across diverse models and applications.

items.title: Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2603.02604v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning (HACRL), a new Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Reward (RLVR) problem that addresses the inefficiencies of isolated multi-agent on-policy optimization. HACRL enables collaborative optimization with independent execution: heterogeneous agents share verified rollouts during training to mutually improve, while operating independently at inference time. Unlike LLM-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), HACRL does not require coordinated deployment, and unlike on-/off-policy distillation, it enables bidirectional mutual learning among heterogeneous agents rather than one-directional homogeneous teacher-to-student transfer. Building on this problem, we propose HACPO, a collaborative RL algorithm that enables principled rollout sharing to maximize sample utilization and cross-agent knowledge transfer. To mitigate capability discrepancies and policy distribution shifts, HACPO introduces four tailored mechanisms with theoretical guarantees on unbiased advantage estimation. Extensive experiments across diverse heterogeneous model combinations and reasoning benchmarks show that HACPO consistently improves all participating agents, outperforming GSPO with double rollouts by an average of 3.6% while using only half the rollout cost.

items.title: VLMShield: Efficient and Robust Defense of Vision-Language Models against Malicious Prompts
items.description: arXiv:2604.06502v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) face significant safety vulnerabilities from malicious prompt attacks due to weakened alignment during visual integration. Existing defenses suffer from efficiency and robustness. To address these challenges, we first propose the Multimodal Aggregated Feature Extraction (MAFE) framework that enables CLIP to handle long text and fuse multimodal information into unified representations. Through empirical analysis of MAFE-extracted features, we discover distinct distributional patterns between benign and malicious prompts. Building upon this finding, we develop VLMShield, a lightweight safety detector that efficiently identifies multimodal malicious attacks as a plug-and-play solution. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior performance across multiple dimensions, including robustness, efficiency, and utility. Through our work, we hope to pave the way for more secure multimodal AI deployment. Code is available at [this https URL](https://github.com/pgqihere/VLMShield).

items.title: U-STS-LLM: A Unified Spatio-Temporal Steered Large Language Model for Traffic Prediction and Imputation
items.description: arXiv:2605.11735v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate spatio-temporal cellular traffic analysis is fundamental to the reliable operation of modern mobile networks, as it underpins load forecasting for congestion avoidance and missing-data imputation for continuity despite transmission errors. While deeply connected, forecasting and imputation have historically evolved as separate sub-fields. Existing models are typically task-specific, decouple temporal and spatial modeling, and rely on cascaded designs that accumulate errors and latency. Meanwhile, adapting pre-trained LLMs for this domain often leaves spatial structure under-guided and tends to overfit on limited data. To bridge these gaps, we propose U-STS-LLM, a unified framework built on a partially frozen spatio-temporally attentive (PFSTA) LLM backbone. A Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Attention Bias Generator synthesizes a persistent functional graph with transient nodal states to steer attention, while a lightweight parallel branch yields a stable local estimate fused via a Gated Adaptive Fusion, confining the LLM to residual correction. Trained under a unified multi-task objective, the model attains state-of-the-art results with low trainable-parameter overhead. Extensive experiments on real-world cellular traffic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of U-STS-LLM, achieving average RMSE improvements of 23.7% over the strongest baselines in forecasting and 13.1% in imputation, with further gains exceeding 33% in zero-shot transfer to unseen network regions.

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models for Credit Risk Prediction: A Dedicated Review and Empirical Comparison
items.description: arXiv:2605.18147v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predictive models are central to credit risk management, where the accuracy of default-probability and loss estimates affects the profitability of lending and the stability of the financial system. Decades of benchmarking research have consolidated the state of the art, with gradient-boosting models often representing the strongest machine-learning benchmark, while linear and logistic models remain important regulatory and industry reference models. The recent advent of tabular data foundation models introduces a new paradigm for predictive modeling. Rather than fitting a model to a target dataset, they use in-context learning to integrate information from the target dataset with prior knowledge acquired through large-scale pretraining on diverse collections of (synthetic) tabular data. We conjecture that access to information beyond the target data is beneficial in small-data settings and may help address longstanding challenges, including low-default portfolios. Whether this promise holds in practice remains an open question. This paper benchmarks state-of-the-art tabular foundation models against a broad set of classical and advanced machine learning competitors on two core tasks: Probability of Default (PD) and Loss Given Default (LGD) modeling. We evaluate $33$ classification methods across $14$ PD datasets and $27$ regression methods across $7$ LGD datasets, spanning a range of performance indicators and experimental conditions. The most recent tabular foundation models, in particular TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2, achieve the strongest average results, with the largest gains in small-sample and strongly imbalanced settings. These results are notable because these models are used with their pretrained parameters fixed and without downstream hyperparameter optimization or task-specific parameter updates.

items.title: Regret-Based $(\epsilon,\delta)$-optimal Stopping Criteria for Bayesian Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2605.22561v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a widely used iterative black-box optimization method that utilizes Gaussian process (GP) surrogate models. In practice, BO is typically terminated after a fixed evaluation budget is exhausted, which can incur unnecessary cost and provides no optimality guarantee on solution quality. Recent research in developing a practical stopping criterion has made empirical progress, yet a theoretically sound stopping criterion remains a work in progress.
